
--- PAGE 1 ---
Mechanical Factors Contributing to Altered Knee Extension
Moment during Gait after ACL Reconstruction: A Longitudinal
Analysis
Chandramouli Krishnan1,2,3,4,6, Alexa K. Johnson2, Riann M. Palmieri-Smith2,5
1Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Michigan Medicine, Ann Arbor, MI;
2School of Kinesiology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI;
3Robotics Institute, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI;
4Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI;
5Department of Orthopedic Surgery, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI
6Physical Therapy Department, College of Health Sciences, University of Michigan-Flint, Flint, MI
Abstract
Purpose: To comprehensively examine the extent to which knee flexion angle at initial contact,
peak knee flexion angle, and vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) contribute to knee extension
moments during gait in individuals with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction.
Methods: Overground gait biomechanics were evaluated in twenty-six participants with ACL
reconstruction at three timepoints (about 2 months, 4 months, and 6 months after the surgery).
Knee flexion angle at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, peak vGRF, and peak knee
extension moment were calculated for each limb during the early stance phase of gait for all three
timepoints. A change score from baseline (timepoint 2−timepoint 1 and timepoint 3−timepoint
1) along with limb symmetry values (ACL−non-ACL limb values) were also calculated for these
variables. Multiple linear regressions utilizing classical and Bayesian interference methods were
used to determine the contribution of knee flexion angle and vGRF to knee extension moment
during gait.
Results: Peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF positively contributed to knee extension
moment during gait in both the reconstructed (R2 = 0.767, p<0.001) and non-reconstructed limbs
(R2 = 0.815, p<0.001). Similar results were observed for the symmetry values (R2 = 0.673,
p<0.001) and change scores (R2 = 0.731–0.883; all p<0.001), except that the changes in knee
flexion angle at initial contact also contributed to the model using the change scores in the
non-reconstructed limb (timepoint 2−timepoint 1: R2 = 0.844, p<0.001; timepoint 3−timepoint 1:
Address for Correspondence: Chandramouli Krishnan, PT, PhD, University of Michigan, 325 E Eisenhower Parkway, Suite 3013,
Ann Arbor, MI – 48108; Phone: (319)-321-0117; Fax: (734)-615-1770; mouli@umich.edu.

R2 = 0.883, p<0.001). Bayesian regression evaluating the likelihood of these prediction models
showed that there was decisive evidence favoring the alternative model over the null model (all
Bayes Factors [BF10]>1000). Standardized beta coefficients indicated that changes in knee flexion
angle had a greater impact (>2x) on knee extension moments than vGRF at both timepoints in both
limbs (βvGRF = 0.204–0.309; βkneeflexion= 0.703–0.831).
Conclusions: The findings indicate that both knee flexion angle and peak vGRF positively
contribute to altered knee extension moments during gait, but the contribution of knee flexion
angle is much greater than vGRF. Therefore, treatment strategies targeting these variables may
improve knee loading after ACL reconstruction.
Keywords
KNEE MOMENT; KNEE KINETICS; JOINT LOADING; KNEE ANGLE; LIGAMENT
INJURY; SPORTS
INTRODUCTION
Restoration of normal gait patterns is a major clinical goal when rehabilitating individuals
with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. However, despite significant
rehabilitation efforts to normalize gait patterns, several studies show that altered knee
biomechanics is commonplace after ACL reconstruction (1–4). Specifically, knee joint
underloading during walking (as measured by knee moments or contact forces) has been
identified as a significant issue in these individuals due to the growing evidence that
points to its association with the development of post-traumatic osteoarthritis after ACL
reconstruction (5–8). These deficits in knee joint loading are seen as early as 2–3 months
following surgery and persist for years after the surgery (9–12). Hence, early interventions
that target altered knee loading could potentially improve the long-term knee health after
ACL reconstruction. However, a critical step before developing new interventions to combat
post-ACL reconstruction knee loading deficits is to identify the mechanical factors that
contribute to these deficits.
Several mechanical and neuromuscular factors can contribute to altered knee loading during
gait. Neuromuscular factors such as quadriceps weakness and dysfunction (e.g., arthrogenic
muscle inhibition) may alter knee joint loading indirectly by altering the ability of the knee
to properly attenuate forces during the loading phase of the gait (13). In contrast, mechanical
factors such as knee flexion angle and vertical ground reaction forces (vGRFs) could directly
influence knee joint loading, as they serve as primary inputs to the calculation of knee
joint moments and contact forces (9). While previous research on the role of neuromuscular
factors on knee joint loading has been conflicting (13–15), there has been a consistent
link between mechanical factors and knee joint loading. For example, previous research
indicates that reduced vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) in the ACL-reconstructed limb
is strongly associated with reduced knee extensor moments in the ACL-reconstructed limb
and that modulation in vGRF alters knee moments during gait (9, 10). Similarly, there is
a moderate positive association between knee flexion angle and knee moments during gait
after ACL reconstruction (9). These findings have instigated researchers to use biofeedback
to improve knee moments and restore normal gait patterns after ACL reconstruction (16).
Krishnan et al. Page 2
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 3 ---
While previous research has established the cross-sectional association between vGRF,
knee flexion angle, and the knee moment during gait, the longitudinal nature of this
relationship is currently unknown. In other words, is the change in vGRF and knee flexion
angle with time associated with the change in knee moment with time? Moreover, the
extent to which changes in knee angle and vGRF asymmetry between limbs with time
contribute to changes in knee moment asymmetry is not clear. Further, prior studies have
used classical hypothesis testing based on p-values, which is often affected by small
sample size and does not answer the primary research question of interest – what is the
probability of the null hypothesis being true given the observed data? These are crucial
gaps that need to be filled before implementing any targeted intervention to address
altered knee loading after ACL reconstruction. Therefore, the purpose of this study was
to comprehensively (both cross-sectionally and longitudinally) examine the extent to which
knee flexion angle at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, and vGRF contribute to
knee extension moments during gait in individuals with ACL reconstruction. Participants
were evaluated at three timepoints: about 1) 2 months after ACL reconstruction, 2) 4
months after ACL reconstruction, and 3) 6 months after ACL reconstruction. Cross-sectional
analyses were performed using the normalized raw data and the symmetry values (ACL
limb−non-ACL limb) from all timepoints. Longitudinal analyses were performed at the
4-month and 6-month timepoints using the change scores from baseline (i.e., timepoint
2−timepoint 1 and timepoint 3−timepoint 1). We hypothesized that knee flexion angle at
initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, and vGRF would be positively associated with
peak knee extension moment and significantly contribute to altered knee loading during gait
both cross-sectionally and longitudinally. These hypotheses were evaluated both using the
traditional p-values obtained from classical hypothesis testing and Bayes factors obtained
from Bayesian statistics.
METHODS
Participants
Twenty-six individuals (17 females, 9 males; Age: 20.7±5.6 years; Height: 1.72±0.10
meters (m), Body mass: 70.0±12.0 kilograms (kg), Body mass index: 23.6±3.6 kg/m2) with
ACL reconstruction (21 bone-patellar tendon-bone graft, 4 hamstring tendon graft, and 1
quadriceps tendon graft) volunteered to participate in this study. Participants were part of
a clinical trial (NCT03282565) that examined the effects of functional resistance training
on knee strength and biomechanics after ACL reconstruction and were tested at three
timepoints: about 1) 2 months after ACL reconstruction (2.2±0.7 months), 2) 4 months after
ACL reconstruction (4.6±0.8 months), and 3) 6 months after ACL reconstruction (6.7±0.8
months). Participants in both the intervention and control arms of the study were included
to ensure that there was enough spread in the data for regression analyses. Participants were
included if they 1) were aged 14–40 years old, 2) had suffered an acute, primary, unilateral
complete ACL rupture, and 3) had undergone ACL reconstruction with an autograft.
Participants were excluded from the study if they 1) had suffered a previous ACL injury or
previous surgery to either knee, 2) had sustained a recent significant knee injury other than
the ACL tear, 3) had sustained a bony fracture or knee dislocation accompanying their ACL
injury, 4) were pregnant or planning to become pregnant, 5) had a medical condition (e.g.,
Krishnan et al. Page 3
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 4 ---
a history of uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension) that could negatively affect the study
results, and/or 6) were unable to provide written informed consent. All participants read
and signed an informed consent/assent document approved by the University of Michigan
Medical Institutional Review Board before their participation. Parental consent was obtained
if the participant was a minor child.
Gait Biomechanics Testing
Overground knee biomechanical gait data were collected using a 15-camera motion capture
system (MX-13, Vicon Motion System Ltd., Oxford, GBR) and two independent force
plates (AMTI OR6–7, Advanced Mechanical Technology Inc., Watertown, MA, USA)
embedded on level ground. Motion capture data (240Hz) were synchronized with GRF data
(1200Hz) using Vicon hardware/software. A total of 34 reflective markers (14 mm diameter)
were placed bilaterally over the participant’s anatomical locations (17). A static trial of each
participant aligned within the laboratory coordinate system was recorded, following which
walking trials were performed. Five trials were collected at the participant’s self-selected
gait speed during all three testing sessions and were used in further analysis. Participants
were instructed to walk at their comfortable, habitual walking pace. Marker data and ground
reaction forces were filtered with a zero phase-lag low-pass Butterworth filter (4th order,
12 Hz cut-off). Visual 3D software (v3.90, C-Motion, Rockville, MD, USA) was used
to calculate bilateral knee sagittal plane flexion-extension motions and internal moments.
Lower limb joint rotations were calculated using the Cardan rotation sequence and were
expressed relative to each participant’s neutral static position recorded during the static
trial. Joint moments were normalized to the participant’s height and mass (obtained at each
timepoint) and vGRF was normalized to the participant’s body weight. All biomechanical
data were time normalized to the stance phase of the gait cycle, with the initial contact
and toe-off being defined using a vGRF threshold of 10 N (18). The ensemble averages
of the time-normalized knee angle, vGRF, and knee moment data were used in further
analyses. Knee flexion angle at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, peak vGRF, and
peak knee extension moment were calculated for each limb during the early stance phase
of gait, identified as the first 50% of the stance phase, for all three timepoints (Figure 1)
(15). We chose the first 50% of the stance phase for two reasons: (1) Most of the prior
research in ACL-reconstructed population has almost exclusively focused on the peak knee
moment during the loading response/early stance, and (2) this is also the region where
individuals with ACL reconstruction typically exhibit differences in gait mechanics when
compared with uninjured controls. A change score (timepoint 2−timepoint 1 and timepoint
3−timepoint 1) along with limb symmetry values (i.e., ACL limb values−non-ACL limb
values) were also calculated for these variables.
Statistical Analyses
All statistical analyses were performed using the JASP version 0.14.0.0 statistical software
(https://jasp-stats.org/), and the JASP outputs are provided in Appendix 1 and in the Open
Science Framework (OSF - https://osf.io/zxkes/). Descriptive statistics were computed for
each variable, and rain cloud plots were generated for robust data visualization (19).
Stepwise multiple linear regression analysis was used to determine the contribution of
knee flexion angle at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle during early stance, and
Krishnan et al. Page 4
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 5 ---
peak vGRF during early stance to knee joint loading (i.e., peak knee moment) during the
early stance phase of gait. Separate regression analyses were performed using the data
from the reconstructed limb, non-reconstructed limb, symmetry values, and the change
scores to comprehensively understand the contributions of knee flexion angle and vGRF
to peak knee extension moment during gait. We adopted an inclusive statistical approach
where both classical and Bayesian regression analyses were performed to measure statistical
significance (p-value) and the Bayes Factor (BF10), respectively (20–25). More details
regarding the Bayesian analysis and how to interpret the results of this analysis are provided
in the JASP manual:(http://static.jasp-stats.org/Manuals/Bayesian_Guide_v0_12_2_1.pdf).
Briefly, Bayesian regression analyses in JASP were conducted using the default prior to
compute BF10 that describes the likelihood of the alternative model (β ≠ 0) to the likelihood
of the null model (β = 0). Thus, the BF10 indicates the relative strength of evidence in the
data for two competing hypotheses. We used the descriptive classifications adopted by JASP
(based Jeffreys’s scheme (26)) to identify Bayes Factor values as none, anecdotal, moderate,
strong, very strong, or decisive relative evidence for our alternative hypothesis (Table 1).
The Volk-Selke Maximum p-Ratio (VS-MPR) was also computed to estimate the maximum
possible odds in favor of the alternative hypothesis (H1) over the null hypothesis (H0), based
on a two-sided p-value (27, 28). This was computed using the following equation:
VS‐MPR =
1
−e × p × ln p
forp ≤ 0.37
A significance level of α = 0.05 was used for classical regression analyses.
RESULTS
Raw Scores
Raincloud plots showing the distributions of knee flexion angle at initial contact, peak knee
flexion angle, peak vGRF, and peak knee extension moment for the ACL-reconstructed and
non-ACL-reconstructed limbs at the three timepoints are shown in Figure 2. Regression
analyses indicated that peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF together significantly
predicted peak knee extension moment during gait in both the reconstructed (p < 0.001, R2
= 0.767, VS-MPR = 1.702e +21; Figure 3A) and the non-reconstructed limbs (p < 0.001, R2
= 0.815, VS-MPR = 7.616e +24; Figure 3B). Bayesian regression evaluating the likelihood
of these prediction models showed that there was decisive evidence favoring the alternative
regression model that included peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF as opposed to the
null model that only included the intercept (ACL BF10 = 8.463e +20 and non-ACL BF10 =
3.607e +24).
Limb Symmetry Values
Raincloud plots showing the distributions of limb symmetry values for knee flexion angle
at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, peak vGRF, and peak knee extension moment
at the three timepoints are shown in Figure 4. Regression analyses indicated that peak
knee flexion angle symmetry and peak vGRF symmetry together significantly predicted
peak knee extension moment symmetry during gait (p < 0.001, R2 = 0.673, VS-MPR =
Krishnan et al. Page 5
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 6 ---
8.197e +15; Figure 3C). Bayesian regression evaluating the likelihood of these prediction
models showed that there was decisive evidence favoring the alternative regression model
that included peak knee flexion angle symmetry and peak vGRF symmetry as opposed to the
null model that only included the intercept (BF10 = 4.390e +15).
Change Scores
Raincloud plots showing the distributions of changes (from timepoint 1) in knee flexion
angle at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, peak vGRF, and peak knee extension
moment for the ACL-reconstructed and non-ACL-reconstructed limbs at timepoints 2 and
3 are shown in Figure 5. When evaluating the reconstructed limb, regression analyses
indicated that the changes in peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF together significantly
predicted the changes in peak knee extension moment during gait at both timepoint 2
(p < 0.001, R2 = 0.775, VS-MPR = 606628.184; Figure 6A) and timepoint 3 (p <
0.001, R2 = 0.731, VS-MPR = 47973.267; Figure 6C). Bayesian regression evaluating the
likelihood of these prediction models showed that there was decisive evidence favoring
the alternative regression model that included changes in peak knee flexion angle and
peak vGRF as opposed to the null model that only included the intercept (ACL BF10 at
timepoint 2 = 329729.448 and ACL BF10 at timepoint 3 = 27481.216). When evaluating the
non-reconstructed limb, regression analyses indicated that the changes in knee flexion angle
at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, and peak vGRF together significantly predicted
the changes in peak knee extension moment during gait at both timepoint 2 (p < 0.001, R2 =
0.844, VS-MPR = 4.129e +6; Figure 6B) and timepoint 3 (p < 0.001, R2 = 0.883, VS-MPR
= 3.068e +7; Figure 6D). Bayesian regression evaluating the likelihood of these prediction
models showed that there was decisive evidence favoring the regression model that included
changes in peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF as opposed to the null model that only
included the intercept (non-ACL BF10 at timepoint 2 = 2.526e +6 and non-ACL BF10 at
timepoint 3 = 1.779e +7).
DISCUSSION
This study was performed to evaluate the extent to which knee flexion angle and
vGRF contribute to knee extension moment during walking in individuals with ACL
reconstruction. As hypothesized, both peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF significantly
contributed to peak knee extension moment during the early stance phase of gait.
Specifically, these variables explained more than 75% of the variance in the peak knee
extension moment data in both the ACL-reconstructed and the non-ACL-reconstructed
limbs. While the amount of variance explained by the model reduced slightly when using the
symmetry values, peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF symmetry values still explained
more than 67% of the variance in peak knee extension moment symmetry. More importantly,
the longitudinal changes in peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF explained about 73%
to 84% of the variance in peak knee extension moment changes after ACL reconstruction.
The Bayes factors (BF10) and VS-MPR values for each of these predictive models were also
extremely high (>10,000), indicating that the evidence in favor of the alternative predictive
models over the null model was decisive. Collectively, these findings indicate that alterations
in knee kinematics (peak knee flexion angle) and kinetics (vGRF) contribute to altered knee
Krishnan et al. Page 6
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 7 ---
loading (knee extension moments) during gait and emphasize the importance of developing
targeted interventions that improve knee kinematics and kinetics to restore normal gait
mechanics after ACL reconstruction.
Individuals with ACL reconstruction exhibit abnormal gait patterns (e.g., reduced GRFs and
knee flexion angle) that do not recover even years after surgery and rehabilitation (1–4).
These altered gait patterns have been shown to contribute to abnormal knee loading (e.g.,
reduced knee moment) and poor knee function after ACL reconstruction and have been
linked to the pathogenesis of posttraumatic osteoarthritis (5, 6, 9, 10, 29, 30). Accordingly,
researchers have placed considerable efforts to develop new interventions targeting abnormal
knee loading in individuals with ACL reconstruction. However, a clear understanding of
the mechanical factors that contribute to altered knee loading after ACL reconstruction is
critical to developing appropriate intervention strategies. The results of this study indicate
that peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF during early stance contribute significantly
to the peak knee extension moment during gait, which is consistent with previous cross-
sectional research showing that reduced GRFs and knee flexion range of motion are strongly
associated with reduced knee extensor moments 3–4 months after ACL reconstruction (9).
Interestingly, when evaluating the standardized coefficients, it appears that the peak knee
flexion angle contributes to a much larger extent (>2x) than the peak vGRF to the observed
knee extension moments during gait (see Appendix, Supplemental Digital Content 1). This
finding suggests that interventions that target to increase knee flexion angles may have a
higher impact on improving knee joint loading than interventions that target to increase
vGRF. Knee flexion angles are also easier to target in a clinic due to the increasing
availability of low-cost camera systems that can provide real-time feedback of knee joint
angles (31–33). However, further research is warranted to determine if targeting greater knee
flexion angle during gait can improve knee joint loading and cartilage health following ACL
reconstruction.
There are two novel aspects to this study. First, unlike previous studies, we performed
a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between vGRF, knee flexion angle, and
peak knee moment. Specifically, we evaluated the ability of peak vGRF and peak knee
flexion angle to predict peak knee extension moment cross-sectionally using individual limb
data and symmetry values. We also examined the relationships between these variables
longitudinally to understand how a change in one variable contributes to the other. This
information is critical because a strong initial correlation between vGRF, knee flexion
angle, and knee moment does not necessarily imply that these variables will also follow
a similar trend of improvement with time (or training), which can be determined using a
change/gain score (i.e., changes across timepoints) (34). Here, using a change score, we
show for the first time that changes in vGRF and peak knee flexion angle predict changes
in peak knee extension moment in individuals with ACL reconstruction. These findings
suggest that the correlations seen between these variables can be inferred as causative, and
hence, interventions improving knee flexion angle and vGRF early after ACL reconstruction
could lead to sustained improvements in knee joint loading. Second, we also used a
novel Bayesian approach that evaluated the likelihood of these predictive models given
the observed experimental data. Unlike traditional hypothesis testing based on p-values,
Bayesian analysis provides evidence related to the likelihood of two competing hypotheses
Krishnan et al. Page 7
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 8 ---
(null and alternative) and allows inferences to be made about whether the observed data is
more consistent with the alternative hypothesis or the null hypothesis. The results of this
study indicated that the Bayes Factors were very high (>1000), indicating decisive evidence
favoring our predictive model over the null model. As indicated before, these are critical
findings that strengthen the existing cross-sectional literature and provide a step in the right
direction to develop interventions that could potentially address abnormal gait biomechanics
after ACL reconstruction.
There are some limitations to this study. One limitation is that we only evaluated the
mechanical factors that contribute to peak knee extension moments during gait. However,
other factors such as graft type, knee pain, and gait speed can contribute to altered knee
moments after ACL reconstruction. We do note that knee angle and vGRF contributed to
more than 70% of the variation in peak knee extension moments; thus, the contributions
of other variables that were not included in the analyses must be only minimal. Another
limitation is that we only evaluated the peak knee extension moments during the first
50% of the stance phase. This was an intentional choice because previous studies have
primarily focused on peak knee moments during the loading response/early stance phase of
the gait, where individuals with ACL reconstruction exhibit differences in gait mechanics
when compared with uninjured controls. However, it is likely that knee moments during
the latter part of the stance phase may also be crucial to the development of post-traumatic
knee osteoarthritis and need to be evaluated in future studies. Finally, while we evaluated
the causal association of knee flexion angle and vGRF with knee extension moment during
gait, we do not know whether improvements in knee flexion angle and vGRF would lead
to sustained improvements in knee moments during gait. Future studies are warranted to
examine this important research question, as it has implications for improving gait function
after ACL reconstruction.
CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, the results of this study indicated that peak knee flexion angle and vGRF
significantly predicted peak knee extension moment in individuals with ACL reconstruction,
both cross-sectionally and longitudinally. Specifically, cross-sectional analyses using the
normalized raw values and symmetry values from all timepoints indicated that peak knee
flexion angle and peak vGRF together contributed positively to knee extension moment
during gait. In addition, longitudinal analyses using change scores from baseline indicated
that changes in peak knee flexion angle and vGRF with time predicted changes in peak
knee extension moment, with knee flexion angle influencing knee extension moment more
than vGRF in both limbs at both timepoints. Bayesian regression indicated that there was
decisive evidence favoring the likelihood of these prediction models. These results suggest
that treatment strategies targeting greater knee flexion angle and vGRF may improve knee
loading after ACL reconstruction.

Figure 1:
An exemplary data of sagittal plane knee kinematics, vertical ground reaction force (vGRF),
and knee moment from a participant in our study to depict the region at which the analysis
was performed. The solid lines represent the anterior cruciate ligament-reconstructed limb
(ACL), and the broken lines represent the non-ACL-reconstructed limb (Non-ACL). Ellipses
represent the point at which gait data were evaluated: knee flexion angle at initial contact,
peak knee flexion angle, peak vGRF, and peak knee extension moment during the early
stance phase of gait when the knee is maximally loaded.
Krishnan et al. Page 12
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 13 ---
Figure 2:
Raincloud plots showing distributions of (A) knee flexion angle at initial contact, (B) peak
knee flexion angle, (C) peak vertical ground reaction force (vGRF), and (D) peak knee
extension moment during early stance for the ACL-reconstructed limb (ACL) and non-ACL-
reconstructed limb (Non-ACL) at the three timepoints (about 2 months, 4 months, and 6
months post-surgery) tested in this study. The circles on the plot indicate individual data
points for the reconstructed and the non-reconstructed limbs at timepoint 1 (1), timepoint
2 (2), and timepoint 3 (3). Rainclouds and notched box plots show the distribution of the
data, and the horizontal line on the box plot indicates the mean of the distribution. Note that
a lower knee angle at initial contact (A) indicates that the participant walked with a more
extended knee at heel strike, and a lower peak knee angle (B) indicates that the participant
walked with reduced knee flexion during the early stance phase.
Krishnan et al. Page 13
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

--- PAGE 14 ---
Figure 3:
(A) A scatterplot of actual vs. predicted knee moments of the ACL-reconstructed limb
(ACL) using the regression model that used peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF
during early stance in the ACL-reconstructed limb. (B) A scatterplot of actual vs. predicted
knee moments of the non-ACL-reconstructed limb (Non-ACL) using the regression models
that used peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF during early stance in the non-ACL-
reconstructed limb. (C) A scatterplot of actual vs. predicted knee moment symmetry (i.e.,
ACL limb values−non-ACL limb values) using the regression model that used peak knee
flexion angle and peak vGRF symmetry values during early stance.

--- PAGE 15 ---
Figure 4:
Raincloud plots showing distributions of symmetry values (i.e., ACL-reconstructed limb
values−non-ACL-reconstructed limb values) for (A) knee flexion angle at initial contact, (B)
peak knee flexion angle, (C) peak vertical ground reaction force (vGRF), and (D) peak knee
extension moment during early stance for the ACL-reconstructed limb (ACL) and non-ACL-
reconstructed limb (Non-ACL) at the three timepoints (about 2 months, 4 months, and 6
months post-surgery) tested in this study. The circles on the plot indicate individual data
points for the reconstructed and the non-reconstructed limbs at timepoint 1 (1), timepoint 2
(2), and timepoint 3 (3). Rainclouds and notched box plots show the distribution of the data,
and the horizontal line on the box plot indicates the mean of the distribution. Note that a
negative Δ value in limb symmetry indicates that the ACL-reconstructed limb had a lower
value than the non-ACL-reconstructed limb, and vice versa for a positive Δ value.

--- PAGE 16 ---
Figure 5:
Raincloud plots showing distributions of change scores (i.e., changes across timepoints) for
(A) knee flexion angle at initial contact, (B) peak knee flexion angle, (C) peak vertical
ground reaction force (vGRF), and (D) peak knee extension moment during early stance
for the ACL-reconstructed limb (ACL) and non-ACL-reconstructed limb (Non-ACL) at the
three timepoints (about 2 months, 4 months, and 6 months post-surgery) tested in this
study. The circles on the plot indicate individual data points for the reconstructed and the
non-reconstructed limbs at timepoint 2 (2−1) and timepoint 3 (3−1), and timepoint 3 (3).
Rainclouds and notched box plots show the distribution of the data, and the horizontal
line on the box plot indicates the mean of the distribution. Note that a negative Δ value
in the change score indicates that the baseline value (timepoint 1) had a higher value than
timepoint 2 or 3, and vice versa for a positive Δ value.
Krishnan et al. Page 16

--- PAGE 17 ---
Figure 6:
(A) Scatterplots of actual vs. predicted changes in knee moment of the ACL-reconstructed
limb (ACL) and non-ACL-reconstructed limb (Non-ACL) using regression models that
used changes in knee flexion angle at initial contact, peak knee flexion angle, and peak
vGRF during early stance of the respective limbs across timepoints. Note that the ACL-
reconstructed limb had peak knee flexion angle and peak vGRF as predictors in the model
whereas the non-ACL-reconstructed limb had knee flexion angle at initial contact, peak knee
flexion angle, and peak vGRF as predictors in the model.

Krishnan et al. Page 18
Table 1 –
Interpretation of Bayes Factor (BF10) in favor of alternative hypothesis/model (H1) over null hypothesis/model
(H0).
Bayes Factor (BF10) Interpretation
>100 Decisive evidence favoring the alternative hypothesis/model
30–100 Very strong evidence favoring the alternative hypothesis/model
10–30 Strong evidence favoring the alternative hypothesis/model
3–10 Moderate evidence favoring the alternative hypothesis/model
1–3 Anecdotal evidence favoring the alternative hypothesis/model
1 No evidence favoring the null or the alternative hypothesis/model
1/3–1 Anecdotal evidence favoring the null hypothesis/model
1/10–1/3 Moderate evidence favoring the null hypothesis/model
1/30–1/10 Strong evidence favoring the null hypothesis/model
1/100–1/30 Very strong evidence favoring the null hypothesis/model
<1/100 Decisive evidence favoring the null hypothesis/model
Med Sci Sports Exerc. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2023 December 01.
